procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the Division Bench of the High Court dated 21.12.2017 dismissing the writ petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Appellant filed Application No. 18849 of 2017 under Section 482 Cr.P.C. praying for quashing the criminal proceeding in pursuance of supplementary charge sheet dated 31.05.2017.
2. The High Court disposed of the application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. on 06.07.2017, directing the appellant to surrender before the Special Judge, C.B.I. within two weeks and apply for bail, with an expectation that the bail application would be disposed of expeditiously. The High Court also directed that the non-bailable warrant be kept in abeyance for two weeks.
3. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on 21.12.2017.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture:
1. The appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's order dated 06.07.2017, filed Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No. 7749 of 2017, which was disposed of by the Supreme Court on 24.11.2017, granting further two weeks’ time to the appellant to apply for regular bail before the Special Judge, C.B.I. with a direction to the trial court to consider the said application for bail forthwith.
2. The appellant filed this appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 321 of 2018) against the High Court's judgment and order dated 21.12.2017 dismissing the writ petition.

issue.issue_text: Whether it was obligatory for the Court to release the appellant by accepting the bond under Section 88 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 on the ground that he was not arrested during investigation.

facts: The appellant was not arrested during the investigation phase.
When the appellant appeared in court, he requested to be released by furnishing a bond under Section 88 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
A non-bailable warrant of arrest and proceedings under Sections 82 and 83 of the Cr.P.C. had already been initiated against the appellant.
The appellant had been given liberty by the Supreme Court on two prior occasions to apply for regular bail but had not done so, insisting instead on release under Section 88.
law: The Supreme Court interpreted Section 88 of the Cr.P.C., focusing on the word 'may'.
The Court held that the word 'may' confers a discretionary power upon the court, not a mandatory obligation.
Section 88 does not grant any right to a person who is present in court to be released on bond.
The purpose of this section is to provide the court with a tool to ensure a person's future appearance, not to serve as a substitute for bail provisions.
The power under Section 88 is general and can be used for any person, including witnesses, not just the accused in a case.
application: The Court applied its interpretation of the law to the facts, stating that since Section 88 is discretionary, the lower courts were not obligated to release the appellant.
The Court noted that the appellant was not a "free agent" who could simply choose to appear, as a non-bailable warrant was already pending against him.
Because of the outstanding warrant and proceedings, the Court found that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of Section 88.

The Supreme Court affirmed the decisions of the Special Judge and the High Court, finding that they had provided "cogent reasons" for exercising their discretion to reject the appellant's application.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that it was not obligatory for the court to release him by accepting a bond under Section 88 Cr.P.C. The Court held that Section 88 provides a discretionary power, which the lower courts had correctly exercised by refusing the application, especially since a non-bailable warrant had already been issued against the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it was obligatory for the Court to release the appellant by accepting the bond under Section 88 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 on the ground that he was not arrested during investigation.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's counsel argued that the court should release the appellant by accepting a bond under Section 88 Cr.P.C.

In support of this contention, the counsel referred to two judgments of the Delhi High Court: 'Court on Its own Motion Vs. Central Bureau of Investigation, 109 (2003) Delhi Law Times 494' and 'Sanjay Chaturvedi Vs. State, 132 (2006) Delhi Law Times 692'.
respondent_arguments: The specific arguments of the respondent are not detailed in the provided text.

cases.case_name: Madhu Limaye & Anr. v. Ved Murti & Ors.
cases.principle: Section 91 applies to a person who is present in Court and is a free agent, not to a person who is already under arrest and in custody, as their appearance is not a matter of their own volition.

cases.case_name: State of Kerala & Ors. v. Kandath Distilleries
cases.principle: Section 91 applies to a person who is present in court and is free, not to someone already under arrest and in custody, because their appearance depends on the volition of their custodian, not their own.

cases.case_name: Ramji Missar & Anr. v. State of Bihar
cases.principle: When a statute lays down tests or guidelines for the exercise of discretion by a court, that discretion is not unfettered.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a statute confers a power upon a public officer using enabling language, for the purpose of being used for the benefit of specific persons or for the public good, the exercise of that power is not discretionary but mandatory. Such enabling words, though permissive in form, have a compulsory force, and a court can require the power to be exercised.
obiter: In the 1958 Act, certain tests as a guidance have been laid down for exercise of discretion by the Court, and the submission that there is unfettered discretion was rejected.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's core finding is that the interpretation of Section 88 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which suggests that a court is obligated to accept a bond from a person who was not arrested during investigation, is misconceived and based on an incorrect reading of the statute. The power conferred by Section 88 is discretionary, not mandatory.
legal_tests_applied: The court considered the legal principle for statutory interpretation of when enabling words like 'may' should be construed as compulsory. This occurs when there is 'something in the nature of the thing empowered to be done, something in the object for which it is to be done, something in the conditions under which it is to be done, something in the title of the person or persons for whose benefit the power is to be exercised, which may couple the power with a duty and make it the duty of the person in whom the power is reposed to exercise the power when called upon to do so.'
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument failed because the court explicitly found that their interpretation of Section 88 Cr.P.C. was 'misconceived and based upon incorrect reading' of the law.

The court implicitly rejected the appellant's contention that the power under Section 88 is a 'discretion coupled with duty,' which would make it mandatory. By referencing other statutory provisions where 'may' confers purely discretionary powers, the court distinguished Section 88 from situations where such a duty would arise.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because the court affirmed that the power under Section 88 Cr.P.C. is discretionary for the court to exercise, not an obligation that must be performed upon request.
The court's conclusion that the appellant's reading of the statute was 'misconceived' directly validated the respondent's unstated argument that the court was not required to accept the bond.
